stem.text: Photosynthesis is the energy transfer process that occurs in chloroplasts.

Fig. 5.1 shows some biochemical events that occur in a chloroplast during the light-dependent stage of photosynthesis. Photosystems I and II (PSI and PSII) and some associated proteins of the thylakoid membrane are shown.

stem.caption: Fig. 5.1
stem.alt: Diagram of the thylakoid membrane showing PSII and PSI as ovals within the membrane, a region A above the membrane, a region B below it, electron carrier proteins labelled C between PSII and PSI, light arriving at PSII and PSI, NADP with an arrow to a product D, H+ moving across the membrane, and ADP + Pi converted to ATP by a protein labelled E.

stem.text: A and B are areas of the chloroplast. Name areas A and B.

explanation.text: A is drawn above the thylakoid membrane, which is the stroma, the fluid-filled space surrounding the thylakoids where the Calvin cycle takes place. B is drawn below the membrane, inside the stack, which is the thylakoid lumen (space), where H+ accumulates during the light-dependent reactions.

reasoningChain: Identify the membrane as the thylakoid membrane.
The region outside/above it is the stroma; the region inside/below it (within the thylakoid) is the lumen.

inferredMistakes.text: Swapping the two regions, naming the lumen as the stroma or vice versa.

stem.text: The group of proteins labelled C, PSI and the protein labelled E are involved in a specific biochemical process during the light-dependent stage of photosynthesis.
Name this specific biochemical process and the protein labelled E.

explanation.text: C is the group of electron carrier proteins that receive electrons from PSI and pass them back to PSI (rather than on to NADP), which is the defining feature of cyclic photophosphorylation. E is the protein that uses the H+ gradient built up across the thylakoid membrane to synthesise ATP: ATP synthase.

reasoningChain: Electrons from PSI cycling back to PSI via carrier proteins (C), without involving PSII or NADP, identifies cyclic photophosphorylation.
The protein using the H+ gradient to make ATP is ATP synthase (E).

inferredMistakes.text: Naming non-cyclic photophosphorylation, which would require PSII and reduction of NADP, not just PSI and carrier proteins C.

stem.text: Product D is used during the Calvin cycle.
Identify product D and describe its specific role in the Calvin cycle.

points.text: reduces / gives hydrogen to, glycerate (3) phosphate / GP ;

explanation.text: D is shown forming from NADP after it accepts hydrogen, so D is reduced NADP. In the Calvin cycle, reduced NADP donates its hydrogen to glycerate-3-phosphate (GP), reducing it to triose phosphate (TP), one of the two energy-carrying products of the light-dependent reactions used in the light-independent stage.

reasoningChain: D forms from NADP taking up hydrogen, so D is reduced NADP.
In the Calvin cycle, reduced NADP reduces GP by donating hydrogen to it.
This reduction converts GP into triose phosphate (TP).

inferredMistakes.text: Naming ATP instead of reduced NADP for D, when the diagram specifically shows NADP accepting hydrogen to become D.

stem.text: The rate at which plants use photosynthesis to transfer light energy into chemical energy that is stored in plant biomass can be measured in megajoules per square metre per year (MJ m<sup>–2</sup> yr<sup>–1</sup>).
Fig. 5.2 compares the rates of energy transfer for different ecosystems.

stem.caption: Fig. 5.2
stem.alt: Bar chart of rate of energy transfer in MJ per square metre per year for six ecosystems: tropical forest about 38, temperate forest about 24, snow forest about 15, tropical grassland about 12.5, temperate grassland about 9, desert about 1.

stem.text: Limiting factors affect the rate of photosynthesis.
Describe and suggest how the results for tropical forest, temperate forest and snow forest in Fig. 5.2 show the effect of limiting factors on photosynthesis.

points.text: rate of energy transfer, higher / highest, for tropical or rate of energy transfer, lower / lowest, for snow forest ;
paired data quote with units (at least once) ;
tropical forest has, high(er/est) temperature / hot(ter) ;
tropical forest has high(er/est) light, intensity / duration ;
temperature / light intensity, is a limiting factor (on photosynthesis) ;

markScheme.note: MS 点编号沿用原文（D1/S3/S4/S5 的内容，这里按转录顺序重编为 1–5）。

explanation.text: Reading the chart: tropical forest has the highest rate of energy transfer and snow forest one of the lowest among the three named ecosystems, with actual values quotable from the bars. Tropical regions are warmer and receive more light (both higher intensity and longer duration) than temperate or snow forest regions, and temperature and light intensity are both limiting factors for photosynthesis, so where either is lower, the rate of energy transfer by photosynthesis is lower too.

reasoningChain: Compare the bars: tropical forest highest, snow forest lowest of the three, quoting actual values.
Link the pattern to environmental differences: tropical regions are hotter and receive more light.
Name temperature and light intensity as limiting factors that explain the lower rates in cooler, less sunny ecosystems.

inferredMistakes.text: Describing the pattern in the bar chart without suggesting why it occurs (naming temperature or light as the limiting factor).

stem.text: Suggest reasons why grasslands and desert have a lower rate of energy transfer by photosynthesis than forests.

points.text: stomata shut reducing, carbon dioxide (entry) / gas exchange ;
(so) carbon dioxide (concentration) is a limiting factor ;
(grassland / desert) fewer plants / less plant cover / smaller plants ;
(so smaller surface area) less light absorbed ;

explanation.text: Grasslands and desert are drier environments, so plants there are under more water stress and lose more water by transpiration relative to supply; to conserve water, stomata close more, which also reduces carbon dioxide entering the leaf, making CO2 availability a limiting factor on photosynthesis. These ecosystems also have fewer and smaller plants overall, so less leaf surface area is available to absorb light, further limiting the rate of photosynthesis.

reasoningChain: Drier conditions mean more transpiration relative to water supply, so stomata close more to conserve water.
Closed stomata reduce CO2 entry, making CO2 a limiting factor.
Grassland/desert plant cover is sparser and smaller, giving less total leaf area to absorb light.

inferredMistakes.text: Attributing the lower rate only to "less water" without connecting water stress to stomatal closure and the resulting CO2 limitation.
